title: Draft board, the Army band audition and enlisting
summary: The draft board warns him; recruiters push him to audition for an Army band, and his unusual rudiment earns a 97 and a place in the New York Army Band.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: the final table with the guys with the stamp. And I said I had to have failed, you know. He takes this stamp, I thought he was going to break the table. Bang! Fully qualified for military service. I said, “oh my God.” Here we go man. I mean even my eyes. I mean I used to wear glasses. I had 20/200 vision, a couple surgeries and cataract surgery, I’m 20/20 now you know, except I have to use reading glasses. So anyway, we get back up to Cortland, now my father owned a bar around the corner called the Crystal Hotel. And it was right across the street from the draft board. And I went across to the lady, Helen Wood, the lady at the draft board. I says, “when is this coming?” She says, “it’s coming down man, in a big hurry. You’re going in within a month, or within 60 days, you’re going to be in a military service.” Now I didn’t particularly want to go in the Marines. I mean that was not my first choice. But all of the recruiting guys kept juicing at my father’s bar. So they said, “well you’re a musician, why don’t you try out for the band?” I said, “oh I’m not good enough to be in the Army band.” I mean you know ‘cause you’ve got to — I just didn’t feel as though I was good enough. He says, “well why don’t you take the test anyway?” I said, “okay, all right.” So I went up to the Chimes Building in Syracuse, New York where they did the test. And they put this piece of music on and you have a tape recorder in front of you and you’d play it. You’d have to read the music, sight read it, and do this and that. And you have to play certain rudiments. Now the one thing I learned from my band director, my second band director, Alfred “Corky” Fabrizio, who still is alive and was in drum and bugle corps, was there was a set of rudiments called the “Swiss Army rudiments.” Now they were not popular. In fact, I don’t even know that anybody really even knew them yet in 1965. But he had showed me this one rudiment. I’ll show it to you if you don’t mind. So I get on this tape recorder. It’s just a flam accent, but it’s supposed to alternate, like [drums]. Now alternating, you can only go so fast, because you alternate [drums]. But the way to really, the Swiss Army do it, is you don’t alternate it, you just do it one way [drums]. So now I went in and took this test. So like I’m playing it like I’m doing the alternating thing. And then instead of staying with the alternating as fast as I can go, I mean as fast as is possible to go, I started with the [drums]. Then I quit alternating. I went [drums]. They hadn’t heard Swiss Army rudiments yet. They thought I was playing the flam accent. So when the thing came back, it said — I mean I read all of this stuff and it said score 97, which means superior rating. I means I didn’t have to go to the Army school of music, which was in Rockville, Maryland I think or someplace down there, which at the time I was disappointed. I said I’m going to get a free college education — go two months, get the basic training, actually it’s nine weeks because you’re a week getting your stuff at Fort Dix. But I had to enlist to get this. You are pre-inducted to come right directly to the New York Army band, which was the country club of the Army man. I mean that’s right across from the

Statue of Liberty, right where that thing I showed you there. So I had to enlist for three years in the Army, but that — and you’re guaranteed 14 months. Of course then there’s another 14 to go, that you can get a levy. You don’t get washed out, you are picked for a levy from Washington and it’s okay, somebody’s needed. So I went to basic training and as soon as I got down to Governor’s Island, Fort Jay, Governor’s Island, right across from the Statue of Liberty, the percussion leader, Sgt. Wadkowicz, he dragged me right into that room. He said, “I want to hear that flam accent man.” I said, “well you know I just got out of basic training man, and my chops are a little down.” And I was — I mean when I say it my cover was blown because I couldn’t play it alternating at that speed you know, but they didn’t know the Swiss Army rudiments yet. But anyway, I now was into the New York Army band. Now the New York Army band had guys — everybody that didn’t want to go wanted to be in that band because first of all you’re right in New York City, and second of all you’re not going to Vietnam. And that was the cream of the gigs. But none of the guys in the band were any good at big band stuff, at playing in big bands.
